recommendation: Use Instagram's in-app Professional Dashboard → Best Practices for personalised, account-specific tips on creation, reach, engagement and monetisation before guessing at tactics.
sourceName: Instagram for Creators — Introducing best practices for creators
whyForUnc: An uncle-voice hoops/nutrition creator gets tailored length and cadence guidance from Instagram itself rather than generic algorithm myths.

recommendation: Make Reels people instantly see themselves in — if a viewer thinks "that's literally me," you're on the right track; build content around relatability, not polish.
sourceName: Instagram for Creators — Best practices for creators
whyForUnc: Relatable mindset/nutrition truths in an uncle voice are exactly the "that's me" content Instagram rewards in sub-20s Reels.

recommendation: Record Reels vertical full-screen at 1080×1920px, 9:16 aspect ratio for best quality.
sourceName: Instagram Help Center — Reels
whyForUnc: A phone-shot coaching clip must be true vertical 9:16 so it fills the screen and isn't letterboxed on the Reels feed.

recommendation: Reels can run up to 3 minutes and at least 3 seconds, but keep them short — over-3-minute videos are not recommended to new audiences.
sourceName: Instagram Help Center — Create a reel
whyForUnc: Sub-20s hoops/mindset hits sit safely inside the limit and are the length Instagram pushes hardest to non-followers.

recommendation: Keep your key message, CTA and on-screen text inside the centre “safe zone” — leave roughly the top ~220px and bottom ~450px clear so Instagram's caption, audio and buttons don't cover it.
sourceName: Amplify 11 — Instagram Reels Specs, Safe Zones and Optimization
whyForUnc: A caption like "3 keys to a better handle" must sit mid-frame or the app's UI hides it on a coaching Reel.

recommendation: Export Reels as MP4/MOV with H.264 at 30fps to preserve quality after Instagram re-compresses.
sourceName: Amplify 11 — Instagram Reels Specs and Optimization
whyForUnc: Clean H.264 exports keep a phone-shot drill or meal-prep clip sharp so it doesn't look muddy on the feed.

recommendation: Win the first 3 seconds: open on movement or a bold claim, because roughly half of drop-off happens in the first three seconds of short-form.
sourceName: YouTube Help — Measure key moments for audience retention
whyForUnc: In a sub-20s hoops tip the hook IS the video — the uncle voice has to land the promise before the thumb swipes.

recommendation: Skip the “hey guys, welcome back” intro — a generic greeting tells viewers nothing; front-load the payoff or the surprising claim instead.
sourceName: YouTube Help — Audience retention key moments (intro/first 30s)
whyForUnc: An uncle should jump straight to "stop eating this before training" not a slow intro, or he loses the sub-20s window.

recommendation: Use your retention/“key moments” report: move your strongest moment earlier since audience naturally declines over time, and study “dips” to cut where people leave.
sourceName: YouTube Help — Measure key moments for audience retention
whyForUnc: Lets the coach see exactly which second of a drill clip loses viewers and tighten the next one.

recommendation: Treat “spikes” in retention (rewatched/shared moments) as proof of what resonates — make more content expanding those top segments.
sourceName: YouTube Help — Measure key moments for audience retention
whyForUnc: If a rewatched moment is a specific mindset one-liner, that's the format to spin into a whole series.

recommendation: Treat engagement as a two-way street — reply to comments and interact back, because engagement is measured by likes, comments, saves and shares from real interaction.
sourceName: Instagram for Creators — Create engaging content
whyForUnc: An uncle building a coaching community grows trust by answering "what should my kid eat before a game" in the comments.

recommendation: Layer audio deliberately — Instagram lets you add up to 20 tracks to a single Reel and align them visually while editing.
sourceName: Instagram for Creators — Create engaging content
whyForUnc: Lets the coach stack a voiceover tip over a beat and a ball-bounce sound for a punchy sub-20s clip.

recommendation: Post Reels consistently — use the Best Practices “Creation” guidance on how often to post rather than posting in unpredictable bursts.
sourceName: Instagram for Creators — Best practices for creators
whyForUnc: A steady cadence keeps the coach's account warm between programs so followers expect daily hoops/nutrition hits.

recommendation: Design a scroll-stopping cover/first frame — the opening visual is what people judge, so make frame one clear and striking, not a blurry mid-motion still.
sourceName: Instagram for Creators — Best practices for creators
whyForUnc: A crisp cover of the coach mid-sentence with 3-word text sells the tip on the grid and in Reels.

recommendation: Use Trial Reels: before sharing, tap the toggle to turn on “Trial” so the Reel goes to non-followers first and you can test the idea privately.
sourceName: Instagram for Creators — Trial reels
whyForUnc: Lets the coach test a bold nutrition take on strangers before risking it with his real followers.

recommendation: After about a day, read your Trial Reel's views, likes, comments and shares in the reels viewer and compare against your previous trials before deciding to share it to everyone.
sourceName: Instagram for Creators — Trial reels
whyForUnc: Gives the coach a 24h read on whether a drill idea lands before committing it to his audience.

recommendation: Optionally set a Trial Reel to auto-share — Instagram will push it to your followers if it performs well early (evaluated within the first ~72 hours); you can change this setting anytime.
sourceName: Instagram for Creators — Trial reels
whyForUnc: Automates the winners so a proven hoops tip reaches followers without the coach babysitting metrics.

recommendation: To use Trial Reels your account should be public, a Creator/Business (professional) account, and generally have ~1,000+ followers; if the toggle is missing, update the app and check account type.
sourceName: Instagram Help Center (via Instagram for Creators — Trial reels)
whyForUnc: Tells the coach the exact bar he must clear before the testing feature unlocks for his account.

recommendation: Edit Reels in Meta's free Edits app — it captures up to 10 minutes, has a frame-accurate timeline, and exports with no added watermark.
sourceName: Meta Newsroom — Introducing Edits: A Streamlined Video Creation App
whyForUnc: One free Meta app to cut a coaching clip cleanly and post it watermark-free straight to Reels.

recommendation: Use Edits' real-time insights — including skip rate — to see which parts of a Reel lose viewers and fix the edit before or after publishing.
sourceName: Meta Newsroom — Introducing Edits
whyForUnc: Skip-rate feedback tells the coach the exact second his hoops tip loses people so he can trim the fat.

recommendation: Lean on Edits' inspiration feed of Reels with trending audio plus its high-quality camera and cutout/animation effects to keep production fast.
sourceName: Instagram for Creators — Introducing Edits
whyForUnc: Helps a solo coach find trending sounds and shoot in-app so he can post daily without a studio.

recommendation: Never rely on your camera/phone's built-in mic — it gives “average audio at best”; use an external directional mic (shotgun/cardioid) instead.
sourceName: RØDE — Audio For Film 101: A Vlogger's Guide to Better Sound
whyForUnc: Clear voice is everything for a talking-head mindset coach — viewers tune out instantly on average audio.

recommendation: Get the mic close — proximity is the key to clean audio; keep no more than about two metres between you and the mic when speaking.
sourceName: RØDE — A Vlogger's Guide to Better Sound
whyForUnc: Keeps the coach's voice full and intimate on court or in the kitchen instead of thin and echoey.

recommendation: Turn OFF Automatic Gain Control and set levels manually — aim for peaks around -10dB and never let audio hit 0dB, so it stays comfortably in the minus range.
sourceName: RØDE — A Vlogger's Guide to Better Sound
whyForUnc: Stops the coach's louder "LET'S GO" moments from clipping into distortion mid-Reel.

recommendation: Choose a directional pattern (cardioid/super-cardioid/hyper-cardioid) and use a windshield outdoors to pick up your voice while rejecting court and street noise.
sourceName: RØDE — A Vlogger's Guide to Better Sound
whyForUnc: Outdoor court shoots need wind protection and front-focused pickup so the tip is audible over ambient noise.

recommendation: Light with a 3-point setup: a key light off to one side at ~45°, a dimmer fill on the opposite side to soften shadows, and a backlight behind you to separate you from the background.
sourceName: Vimeo — Your Quick and Dirty Guide to 3-Point Lighting
whyForUnc: Gives a home-studio coach a flattering, professional look instead of flat phone lighting on talking-head Reels.

recommendation: Soften your light — use diffusion/softboxes and move lights closer or farther to control brightness, avoiding harsh unflattering shadows on your face.
sourceName: Vimeo — Your Quick and Dirty Guide to 3-Point Lighting
whyForUnc: Soft even light keeps the coach looking approachable and clear in close-up mindset talks.

recommendation: Read “Views” as every play/replay of your Reel and “Accounts reached” as unique accounts that had it on screen — don't treat views as unique people.
sourceName: Instagram Help Center — View insights on your Instagram reels
whyForUnc: Stops the coach over-reading a high view count — reach tells him how many real people a tip actually touched.

recommendation: Track watch time and average watch time alongside views — they show retention and pacing, i.e. how long people actually stayed, not just that they started.
sourceName: Instagram Help Center — View insights on your Instagram reels
whyForUnc: Average watch time reveals whether the coach's sub-20s tip holds to the end or dies after the hook.

recommendation: Judge Reels on saves and shares, not just likes — these interactions signal the content was useful/worth passing on, which is what a coach wants.
sourceName: Instagram Help Center — View insights on your Instagram reels
whyForUnc: A nutrition tip that gets saved is one parents want to act on later — the strongest signal for a coach.

recommendation: Before posting any photo/video of a child, crop or avoid identifying details — school logos, uniforms, street names and front doors — and never put a child's name, age or school year in the caption.
sourceName: eSafety Commissioner (AU) — Photo and video sharing
whyForUnc: Junior-clinic footage can expose kids' schools/locations — the coach must strip these before posting to a public account.

recommendation: Get consent every time — ask a child before taking their photo and again before sharing it, and respect a no; this models consent and protects them.
sourceName: eSafety Commissioner (AU) — Photo and video sharing
whyForUnc: A coach filming young athletes needs explicit consent from kids and parents before any clip goes public.

recommendation: Accept that sometimes the safest option is not to take or share a photo/video of a child at all — AI tools have sharply escalated the risk of images being harvested and misused.
sourceName: eSafety Commissioner (AU) — Photo and video sharing
whyForUnc: For minors in a coaching program, the coach should default to faces-obscured or no-post rather than risk AI misuse.

recommendation: Publish a clear, up-to-date privacy policy (APP 1) telling people what personal information you collect and how it's handled if your app/site gathers user data.
sourceName: OAIC — Australian Privacy Principles quick reference
whyForUnc: The coach's registration app collects names/emails, so a transparent privacy policy is a baseline legal obligation.

recommendation: Only collect personal information you actually need (APP 3), and apply higher standards to sensitive information such as health/nutrition details.
sourceName: OAIC — Australian Privacy Principles quick reference
whyForUnc: Nutrition/health notes on athletes are sensitive info the coach must collect sparingly and protect more carefully.

recommendation: At the point of collection, tell people what you're collecting and why (APP 5), and only use it for that stated purpose (APP 6) unless you get fresh consent.
sourceName: OAIC — Australian Privacy Principles quick reference
whyForUnc: When the coach signs a player up, he must say why he needs the data and not repurpose it for unrelated marketing.

recommendation: Adopt the National Principles for Child Safe Organisations — embed child safety in leadership and culture (Principle 1) and give children a voice and knowledge of their rights (Principle 2).
sourceName: National Office for Child Safety — National Principles for Child Safe Organisations
whyForUnc: A basketball coach working with juniors is a child-facing organisation and should visibly run to these national principles.

recommendation: Ensure physical AND online environments minimise harm (National Principle 10) and keep families/communities informed and involved (Principle 3) — including how you handle kids' images online.
sourceName: National Office for Child Safety — National Principles for Child Safe Organisations
whyForUnc: Principle 10 explicitly covers online spaces, so the coach's Instagram presence is in scope for child-safe practice.
